stemMd: According to the passage, why does a buyer at the Saturday market have, in practice, no court to turn to over a spoiled wheel of cheese?
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: The town requires traders to settle every complaint before any case can go to court.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Market traders are known to be more honest than other sellers.

options.label: C
options.textMd: The sums involved are too small to make a lawsuit worthwhile.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Courts do not hear disputes about food bought at markets.

options.label: E
options.textMd: Buyers worry that going to court would damage their own reputation.

explanationMd:
The answer is in the sentence that raises the problem. Paragraph 1 says the buyer has "no receipt, no warranty and, in practice, no court to turn to, since the sums involved are too small to be worth a lawsuit." The word "since" introduces the reason directly.

**Check:** notice the qualifier "in practice". The passage does not say a court would refuse the case; it says going to court would cost more than the dispute is worth. Choices that invent a legal rule miss that qualifier.

distractorRationale.a: The passage mentions no town rule about settling complaints. It says traders do replace faulty goods, but as a matter of behaviour, not of regulation.
distractorRationale.b: This is the explanation the passage mentions for why complaints are rare, and the author sets it aside in favour of "a more modest explanation". It does not answer why a court is out of reach.
distractorRationale.d: "In practice" signals a practical obstacle, not a legal bar. The passage gives cost as the reason and never says courts refuse such cases.
distractorRationale.e: Reputation in the passage belongs to traders, not buyers. Nothing suggests that buyers fear for their own good name.
